chapter_theme: The opening of Padumaiyar Ilampakam: freed from prison, Civakan meets both fortunes with equanimity as former deeds, is carried to the god Sudanjanan's mountain, bathed and renamed, hears the god explain that he is the dog Civakan once saved, declines the divine women's offer to win his kingdom for him, and asks to see the world; the god then maps the road ahead, past Jain ascetics washing their karma, a yakshi's welcome, elephant forests, life-drinking ghoul-women, the Pallava country and a burning desert where animals shelter their own.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai; here renamed பவித்திர குமரன்
the god, once the dying dog Civakan helped, who carries him out of prison (called தேவன், விண்ணவன் here)
the god's queens and women (உரிமை, தெய்வ மகளிர்), who bathe Civakan and offer to win his kingdom

1166.reading: The poet turns to ask what the hero of flawless virtue did after the god set him free from the prison none escapes, and promises to tell the deeds of the one whose form, like a figure seen in crystal, no painter could draw.
1166.nuance: The opening verse of Padumaiyar Ilampakam bridges the plot: the rescue (வீட்டரும் சிறையில் தேவன் விடுத்து உயக் கொள்ளப்பட்ட) was told at the end of the previous ilampakam, and the poet now resumes with the hero's travels.

1167.reading: Neither when he lay bound in the great prison nor when the garlanded god came and freed him did grief or joy rise in the hero's heart; he let both go, saying it was the working of former deeds.
1167.event: Civakan, freed from prison by the god, meets both captivity and release without grief or joy, ascribing them to former deeds.

claims.claim: captivity and release alike come from former deeds, so neither calls for grief or joy

1167.nuance: The word is the hero's (ஊழ்வினை என்று விட்டான), and the narrator presents it as his virtue. The plot gives the karma a concrete face: the god who frees him is the dog he helped die well (943-948), as the god says in 1172, so the 'former deed' here is the hero's own act in this very life, not an unknown deed of a past birth. The verse names no school, so the claim is left general.

1168.reading: As a moon bearing the burning sun climbs high, so the god climbed his mountain carrying the hero, a mountain whose streams run thick with flowers, where monkeys and elephants roam and honeycombs hang like moons.
1168.event: The god carries Civakan up to his mountain.
1168.nuance: காய்கதிர் சுமந்து ஓர் திங்கள்: the god is the moon and the hero the sun he carries, which reverses rank and echoes the dog's promised body 'shining like the burning disc of the sun' (காய்கதிர் மண்டலம், 943).

1169.reading: With clear water from the waves of the milk ocean, bright as moonlight, the god had his women bathe the hero in the auspicious way and deck him with jewels, and named the lotus-eyed youth the Holy Prince.
1169.event: The god's women bathe and adorn Civakan with milk-ocean water, and the god names him Pavittira Kumaran.
1169.nuance: பவித்திர குமரன் (the pure or holy prince) is a new name given by the god, in the manner of a consecration bath; it marks the hero's passage from prison to divine favour.

1170.reading: Under a parasol like the full moon on a golden staff, hung with strings of pearls, with maidens waving yak-tail whisks and gem earrings flashing, the hero sat watching the dance to sweet music.
1170.event: Civakan sits in state on the god's mountain, fanned by maidens, watching dance and music.

1171.reading: Seeing the beauty of the garlanded youth, the god's queens felt their unblinking eyes had found their reward, pitied him and asked how the god was bound to him, and the jewelled god answered thus.
1171.event: The god's queens ask him what tie binds him to Civakan.
1171.nuance: இமைப்பிலாப் பயத்தைப் பெற்ற: gods do not blink, and the conceit is that their never-closing eyes are at last put to good use. அளிய (pitiable, dear) may be their pity for his sufferings or simply their tenderness; the verse does not say which.

1172.reading: The god tells them that when he was born among dogs this man removed his suffering, looked on him with grace and gave him this cooled and gracious body, and calls him a bull of countless virtues.
1172.event: Sudanjanan tells his queens that Civakan freed him from his dog's birth and gave him his god's body.
1172.nuance: பிணிக்குலத்து அகவயின் is unusual for 'in the race of dogs'; the sense is clear from the story (941-948) but the wording is not a common name for dogs. The god gives the credit to the man (எனக்கு அருளி), not to the mantra Civakan whispered, so his rescue in 1167 is gratitude repaying a gift; the poem treats the debt of a benefit as the bond between god and man.

1173.reading: The divine women say that they will destroy the hard enmity of this youth, who is like the god with the shark banner, win him the wide earth, establish his marriage with a gentle maiden and give him all of it.
1173.event: The god's women offer to destroy Civakan's enemy, win him the land and marry him to a maiden.
1173.nuance: கடற்சுறவு உயரிய காளை is Kama, whose banner bears the makara; the offer is the whole programme of the rest of the epic (vengeance on Kattiyangaran, the throne, the marriages) handed over as a divine gift, and 1174 shows the hero declining to take it so.

1174.reading: The hero answers that they need not plan how the earth may come to him by taking the enemy's life in battle; if they would give him the lordship of earth and the land of the gods, they are surely able to give it.
1174.event: Civakan answers the divine women's offer.
1174.nuance: The sense of the reply turns on tone. எண்ணல் வேண்டுமோ may mean 'need you trouble to plan it' (he will win the land himself) or simply 'is there any need to think about it' (they can do it at once); the second half (தருகுந் தன்மையீர்) may be courtesy, or a polite deflection that their power could give even heaven, so earth is a small thing he will take on his own. Read with 1175, where he asks only to see the world, the first sense, a refusal of a gift he means to earn, is likelier.

1175.reading: He tells the god that he has one wish: to see the mountains and forests that lie on the earth, the lands and pools hard to reach, and the rivers that cool the eye and the mind.
1175.event: Civakan asks the god's leave to go and see the lands of the earth.

1176.reading: Those who are like fish living in a spring-fed well never set out to taste another land; 'Keep well, I shall go,' the hero said, and the god then told him plainly the nature of the road ahead.
1176.event: Civakan takes leave of the god, who begins to describe the road.

claims.claim: one who never leaves home, like a fish in a well, knows nothing of other lands

1176.nuance: Line 4 (காற்றின தமைதி) is best divided கூறினான் ஆற்றினது அமைதி, 'the nature of the way'; read as காற்றின் (of the wind) it makes poor sense. Lines 1-3 are the hero's speech and line 4 the narrator's; the god's directions fill 1177-1190.

1177.reading: Two kathams beyond this mountain the god says a dark mountain called Aranapatham appears, and at its foot the Caranas wash away their own karma: men who left the cruelty of guarding the earth and renounced without desire.
1177.event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

claims.claim: kings who give up the violence of rule and renounce without desire wash away their own karma by austerity

1177.nuance: சாரணர் are the Jain ascetics with the power of sky-going; the verse makes renunciation a king's turn from rule, which it calls cruelty (தரணி காவல் வெம்மை), and the cleansing is their own act (தம்வினை கழுவுகின்றார்). The scene foreshadows the hero's own end in Mutti Ilampakam.

1178.reading: When the hero bows at the red feet of those whose minds are like the sun, the god says a yakshi of fierce power will appear, receive him as a guest and feed him nectar, and after leaving her he should go to the sandal-wood slopes.
1178.event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.
1178.nuance: The order matters: hospitality from the yakshi (இயக்கி) follows on worship of the ascetics; reverence opens the road.

1179.reading: Five kavathams on, the god says, lies a forest where herds of rutting elephants stay, which no one crosses alone, on the bank of the Ganga that looks like a sea.
1179.event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.
1179.nuance: கங்கை here may be the great river or a name for a local river; the route is a romance geography and the verse does not let one fix it.

1180.reading: Keeping on his right a great joyful pool where lotuses bloom as if fire crept over water and vaalai fish leap like swords, the hero is to go two kathams more.
1180.event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

1181.reading: Past two hills mixed with gems, diamonds and gold like the hero's own shoulders, the god says he will see a great ghoul forest that is decked like women in flowered cloth.
1181.event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

1182.reading: There, says the god to the saffron-chested hero, ghouls like swaying gem-creepers will melt and pine, calling him the thief who stole their beauty by stealth.
1182.event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.
1182.nuance: The ghouls speak the language of a lovesick heroine (களவினின் அணி நலம் கவர்ந்த கள்வ); the deceit is that akam's own words are the lure.

1183.reading: Softening like ripe fruit and burning with desire, they come near saying this is the moment for an embrace, and when they embrace they wring out a man's life and drink it: they are ghouls.
1183.event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

claims.claim: the embrace of a seductive woman who is not what she seems drains a man's life

1183.nuance: The claim is put as a fact of this forest, but it carries the ethic of the warning against deceiving women; the final word (பேய்கள் ஆபவே) unmasks the lovers of 1182.

1184.reading: Leaving the ghoul town and crossing a kavatham, the god says, a land appears beside a golden island washed by white-crested waves, fenced with red paddy and sugarcane, as sweet as coral and the fine-clothed waist of a woman.
1184.event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

1185.reading: That good rich land is called the Pallava country, where the rains never fail their season and lily beds lie like a girdle; if he rests there to ease the toil of the road and then goes on, a stony desert path hard to cross awaits him.
1185.event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

1186.reading: The god says the stones there are like the fine sharp spears of a fierce lord set out over the ground; none but those who know the way pass over them, and the very heat that dwells there would burn the mouth that told of it.
1186.event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.
1186.nuance: The metre changes here. விதி கண்டவர் அல்லது மீது செலார் can mean 'only those who know the rule of the road go over it' or 'only those whose fate has been seen (who are doomed) go there'; வெம்பரன் (a fierce lord, or a hot stone) is also open.

1187.reading: In that heat, the god says, elephants hug their calves and bear the fire themselves lest the young faint, and cock birds fold their hens in their wings and ease their suffering.
1187.event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

1188.reading: Because there is no leaf shade there, the stag, fearing his doe will wither, stands and gives her the shade of his own body and himself melts in the scorching sun, he tells the strong hero.
1188.event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.
1188.nuance: 1187-1188 together are the three tender creatures of the palai tradition (the tusker, the bird with its wings, the stag giving its shadow); the Cintamani shifts the first from the mate to the calf.

1189.reading: Where the must of rutting elephants has dripped on the ground, hooded snakes with bright gems, flashing like a waist-string or lightning, burn and writhe; this is the road, the god says, on which only those foolish in love would set their minds.
1189.event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.
1189.nuance: Line 4 (மடனாம் அயலார் மனம் வைப்பதுவே) is obscure; அயலார் may be strangers to the road or the deluded, and the construal of the snakes in lines 2-3 is also doubtful.

1190.reading: On that road, the god tells the spear-bearing hero, there are matted-haired tapasas who have weakened the hold of the senses and practise austerities, at whose sight those who falter on the road melt in heart.
1190.event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.
1190.nuance: பொறியில் தளர்வார் likely means those who have slackened the senses (ascetics) but could mean those weakened in body; the tapasas (தாபதர், with சடை) are forest ascetics, not the Jain Caranas of 1177, and the poem keeps the two apart.

links.note: The hero calls his release ஊழ்வினை; five verses later the god who freed him explains that Civakan once eased his suffering as a dog and gave him his body.
links.teaches: Read together, the 'former deed' the hero blames is no hidden deed of a past birth but his own recent kindness to a dying dog returning to him, so the epic's karma is visible to the reader while the hero speaks of it as unknown.

links.note: In 943 Civakan promised the dying dog a god's body shining like the sun's disc if it thought on the mantra; in 1172 the god, now in that body, says the man gave it to him.
links.teaches: The promise made through a mantra is remembered by the one who received it as a personal gift of the man, so the epic lets doctrine (the mantra's power) and gratitude (the debt to the giver) both stand as the cause of the rescue.

links.note: Kural 379 asks why those who take good fortune as good should grieve when it turns; Civakan, freed after imprisonment, neither grieves nor rejoices and ascribes both to former deeds.
links.teaches: The epic answers the couplet's question with a stricter ideal: not only bearing ill as one bears good, but declining joy at good fortune too, since rescue is as much karma's working as captivity.

gains.a: the hero's indifference gets a recognised ethical frame, the Kural's reasoning that what fate gives cannot be graded into welcome and unwelcome
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question gets a test case in which the good turn comes through another's hand, a god's, and is still referred to one's own deeds

links.note: Purananuru 192 says good and ill do not come from others, and the speakers neither rejoice that life is sweet nor curse it as bitter; Civakan is freed by a god yet calls the freeing his own former deed and feels neither joy nor grief.
links.teaches: The pair shows the Sangam sage's 'not from others' being kept even when the rescue plainly does come from another: the epic folds the rescuer into the hero's own deed, the dog he once helped.

gains.a: the hero's two-line equanimity is set against a fuller statement of the same stance, with its image of life carried like a raft by the river
gains.b: the poem's abstract claim gets a narrative in which an outside helper exists and the claim must explain him, which it does by tracing the help back to the self

links.note: The Caranas at Aranapatham wash away their own karma (தம்வினை கழுவுகின்றார்) by renouncing rule; Tirumanthiram 2422 says the soul is cleaned of its dirt as cloth by a washer, and everything that comes to it is the bond of grace.
links.teaches: Both use the image of washing a stain from the self, but in the Jain epic the ascetic is the washer and the dirt is his karma, while in Tirumular the washer is grace and even the soul's bonds are its soap; the shared image exposes the rival accounts of who does the cleansing.

gains.a: the Cintamani's brief phrase about karma-washing is shown to carry a doctrine of self-effort that a Saiva reader would contest
gains.b: Tirumular's claim that all is grace's bond is sharpened against a named alternative, ascetics who clean themselves without a god

links.note: Kural 918 says the embrace of deceiving women is an அணங்கு to those without discerning sense; in 1183 the god warns of ghoul-women who come as pining lovers and, embracing, wring out a man's life.
links.teaches: The epic turns the couplet's metaphor into a literal creature of its geography: the deceiving lover really is a life-drinking demon, and what saves the hero is the god's forewarning, standing in for the 'discerning sense' the couplet demands.

gains.a: the ghoul episode is seen to carry the Kural's ethics of the courtesan rather than being a mere marvel of the road
gains.b: the couplet's அணங்கு, which might be read as hyperbole, gets a narrative that spells out what the word threatens: the embrace that kills

links.note: Kalittokai 11 gives the three tender creatures of the burning waste: the tusker who lets his mate drink first, the dove that fans its mate with its wings, the stag that gives its shadow to the shadeless doe; 1187-1188 give the elephant shielding its calf, the cock bird sheltering the hen with its wings, and the stag shading the doe with its body.
links.teaches: The Cintamani keeps the palai triad but changes its use: in the Kalittokai the creatures' care is the heroine's ground for hoping the man will return, while here it only measures the heat for a lone traveller with no beloved at home, so the akam sign of love becomes a road-guide's warning.

gains.a: the god's description is shown to be a set piece of Tamil palai convention, which explains why these three animals and no others appear
gains.b: the Kalittokai's images are seen to outlive their love setting, showing that the triad had become a stock mark of the desert itself

links.note: Konganar's Vaalaik Kummi counts going to foreign lands (தேசாந்திரங்களும் செல்லாதே) among things to avoid, with facing a tiger in the forest and courtesans' ways; Civakan calls those who never leave home fish in a well and sets out, and the god's road then holds elephant forests and ghoul-women.
links.teaches: On the same question, whether to go to other lands, the Siddhar's caution and the hero's resolve give opposite advice, and the epic's road is made of exactly the dangers the Siddhar lists, so the epic treats them as the hero's schooling rather than a reason to stay; the conflict holds only if the kummi's line is read as general advice and not as a rule for the adept alone.

gains.a: the hero's departure is seen as a choice against a known prudential rule, not a mere plot device
gains.b: the kummi's terse prohibition gets its strongest counter-case, a traveller whom the dangers it names do not ruin

source_issues: Verses 1166, 1167 and 1169 were printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 by the build (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verse 1176 line 4 prints கூறினாற் காற்றின தமைதி; the sense requires the division கூறினான் ஆற்றினது அமைதி (the nature of the way).
Verses 1179 and 1180 end line 1 with a full stop (காவதம். / தாமரை.) where the sentence runs on; the stops look like printing artefacts.
Verse 1189 line 4 (மடனாமய லார்மனம் வைப்பதுவே) is obscure and may be corrupt.
